title: The Max K-Armed Bandit: A New Model of Exploration Applied to Search Heuristic Selection
items: k randomized heuristics (arms) on one scheduling problem instance
objective: maximize expected best single sample (best-of-n solution quality) over all trials
evidence: Abstract: 'maximize the expected best single sample reward of the series of trials'
notes: Classic multi-start allocation. Objective is ONE global max over arms (selection/identification), not a sum of per-item curves, so the across-item water-filling theory does not apply; optimum concentrates trials double-exponentially on the observed best arm (Gumbel assumption). Pre-2010 classic, included per brief.

title: The Max K-Armed Bandit: A PAC Lower Bound and tighter Algorithms
objective: find the best single item overall (PAC)
evidence: Abstract: random (uniform) arm choice may be better 'when the maximal rewards of the arms happen to be similar'
notes: Useful analogue: adaptive allocation can lose to uniform/random when arms' maxima are similar (low spread) -- echoes 'spread, not level, governs gain'. Not an across-item sum objective, so NA.

title: Efficient Multi-Start Strategies for Local Search Algorithms
items: multiple local-search runs (algorithm instances) on one objective
objective: best value found overall (global optimum approximation)
evidence: Abstract: 'allocate resources to those instances that could converge to the optimum'
notes: 'Instances' = runs of the local search, not problem instances. Uses an assumed convergence-rate curve g(n) (shape-aware, i.e. marginal-potential signal); compared with explore-and-exploit baselines that use uniform allocation (finite case) or Luby's schedule in the exploration half. Global-max objective -> NA, but it is the closest classical CO analogue of curve-aware allocation.

title: Neural Solver Selection for Combinatorial Optimization
unit: number of neural solvers run per instance (compute)
objective: mean optimality gap (best-of selected solvers) vs time
evidence: Sec 3: 'employ the top-k selection for low-confidence instances to enhance performance'
notes: Rejection-based / top-p strategies give more solvers to instances where the selector is uncertain (softmax-response confidence) and fewer where it is confident; compared against fixed greedy/top-k and a static portfolio. The signal is selector uncertainty (a proxy for the marginal value of an extra solver), not difficulty level, so no E1. The rejection threshold is set as a fraction of test instances ranked by predicted confidence (label-free). p and the rejection ratio are swept on the evaluation set to draw trade-off curves (mild E4 risk, not flagged). Selector inference time is described as orders of magnitude below solver time. Authors leave runtime-aware selection open.
